activities.anchor: The neighbouring categories sharpen the boundary
activities.caption: drag the divider — the neighbours of 'game'
activities.name: gdNeighboursCompare

config.prompt: Two neighbours, two missing clauses — drag the divider:

before.label: Toy
before.text: A ball, a sandbox, a physics playground — play without a defined outcome. No goal.

after.label: Puzzle
after.text: A goal, but static: solved once, its challenge is spent.

config.why: A film has conflict and outcome but no meaningful choices — it plays the same whether you watch closely or not. The sweet spot defining 'game' is a goal pursued through decisions under rules — Sid Meier's 'a series of interesting decisions'.

activities.caption: pair the magic circle's moves with their meanings
activities.name: gdCircleMatch

config.prompt: Inside the agreed bubble, ordinary things carry extra meanings — pair them:

pairs.right: moves carry meanings they have nowhere else
feels like a moral injury, not a mere breach

config.why: Games are among the few places where humans collectively agree to let rules, rather than rank or wealth, define what counts — and the circle's boundary (who agreed to play, and who is being nudged into it) is itself a design surface with ethical weight.

activities.anchor: engagement lives in the narrow channel
activities.caption: pin the flow band on the engagement scale
activities.name: gdFlowPlace

config.prompt: Play stays absorbing only in one band of this scale — pin it:
config.why: Where challenge slightly outruns skill, attention is demanded without anxiety; reverse the overrun and you get boredom on one side, frustration on the other.

activities.anchor: its sign matters more than its strength
activities.caption: file each consequence under its loop
activities.name: gdLoopsSort

config.prompt: File each consequence under the loop that produces it:

items.label: races become foregone conclusions and sessions end early
thrilling in a three-minute match, miserable in a thirty-minute one
outcomes stay uncertain to the wire, quietly devaluing skill

config.why: Balancing these loops — often per game mode, since a tournament and a party night want opposite answers — is systems design at its most consequential, and no amount of content polish repairs a wrong loop.

activities.anchor: a good game is a perfectly fair one
activities.caption: balance the four-player racer
activities.name: gdFairBranch

config.root: You are balancing a four-person racing game. Two philosophies, two sessions.

start.text: Whose evening are you designing for?

choices.label: The sport — the fastest racer should take every race
choices.feedback: Fair rules, neutral outcome — and once the result is decided, three of the four people have stopped racing.

choices.label: The table — keep all four in contest to the last lap
choices.feedback: Bend the outcome instead: best items to the losers, catch-up mechanics, comeback meters — a legitimate goal pure fairness would defeat.

end.text: Fairness of the rules is different from neutrality of the outcome — the question is what each person feels, and for how long.

config.why: Neither loop is 'wrong' — they serve different aesthetics, which is the whole lesson of loop signs.

activities.anchor: its honest history is a retreat from bulk
activities.caption: fill the design document's real job
activities.name: gdDocCloze

config.text: Modern practice prefers living documents: a short concept statement, a description of the core loop, and just enough specified systems to build the next test. The document's job is not completeness but %%0%% — a team arguing about the same game. The single most useful sentence on any page is the core loop's, stated in %%1%%.
config.hint: Two words for what the team must hold in common — and how long the loop statement takes to say.

activities.anchor: Prototyping is where documents meet truth
activities.caption: line up the prototyping ladder, cheap to dear
activities.name: gdPrototypeOrder

config.prompt: Test the loop as cheaply as possible — sequence the ladder from cheapest to dearest:
items: a deck of cards and a hallway — the loop run by hand
a spreadsheet economy playtested at a lunch table
an empty room with two cubes before a level
the full build — art, code and engine work
config.why: Mechanics that feel flat on paper almost never bloom in 3D, and players will use your mechanics in ways you did not plan — which is why the argument ends with a playtest, not the designer.

activities.anchor: prototyping before code is wasted time
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the studio note
activities.name: gdStudioSpot

config.prompt: One line of this studio note is wrong — click it:
lines: Unlike graphics, the interactive layer is just rules — and rules can be run by hand.
A spreadsheet economy can be playtested over a lunch table.
A combat system's pacing can be felt with tokens.
Building first is the cheapest way to learn whether the loop works.
And building first teaches its lesson too late to act on.
config.correction: Building first means paying full price — art, code, engine work — to learn what a deck of cards would have taught in an afternoon.
config.why: The finished game is the real thing, but the loop was testable for pocket change — which is why the field's hard-won rule is to test the loop as cheaply as possible.
